issues.legal_issue: An inspector appointed under a repealed companies law may exercise the investigation powers conferred by the replacement companies law when the appointment remained in force at the replacement law’s commencement.
material_facts: An inspector was appointed under the former companies law to investigate a company’s affairs.
The replacement companies law came into force while the investigation was ongoing, and the appointment remained in force.
The inspector later issued notices requiring attendance, examination on oath, and production of company documents under the replacement law.
issues.conclusion: The inspector was deemed to have been appointed under the replacement law and had authority to issue the notices using its investigation powers.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 645 and 646 of the Companies Act, 1956, are independent and additional saving provisions, not exceptions to one another. Section 645 gives a continuing appointment made under a previous companies law effect as if made under the new Act, insofar as it could have been made under that Act. Section 646 preserves the operation of section 138 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, in specified respects and does not prevent section 645 from applying. Section 652 and section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, were also considered. The inspector appointed under section 138(4) of the former Act was accordingly treated as appointed under section 235 of the new Act and could exercise its section 240 powers.

predicates.company_affairs_investigation: The proceeding involved an investigation into a company’s affairs.
predicates.inspector_appointed_under_prior_company_: The government appointed an inspector under the former companies law to conduct the investigation.
predicates.appointment_in_force_at_replacement_law_: The inspector’s appointment remained in force when the replacement companies law came into effect.

issues.definition: When a company-affairs investigation is ongoing under an appointment made under a prior companies law that remains in force at the start of the replacement law, the inspector may use the replacement law’s investigation powers.

issues.legal_issue: Compelling a person to give evidence or produce documents in a company-affairs investigation does not violate the protection against self-incrimination when no formal accusation of an offence has been made against that person at the relevant time.
material_facts: The inspector was conducting a fact-finding investigation into the affairs of a company and required the managing agent to attend, answer questions on oath, and produce documents.
The investigation could reveal irregularities or offences and could ultimately lead to a prosecution, but it began without an accusation against a specified individual.
At the time the notices were issued, no formal accusation of an offence had been made against the person required to provide evidence.
issues.conclusion: The requirement to give evidence and produce documents did not violate Article 20(3) of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 20(3) protects a person accused of an offence from being compelled to be a witness against himself. A formal accusation relating to the commission of an offence, which may result in prosecution, must exist at the relevant stage. A general fact-finding inquiry into a company’s affairs is not itself an accusation against a specified person, and a possible later prosecution does not retrospectively change the character of the inquiry. The Court relied on Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay, S. A. Venkataraman v. Union of India, M. P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra, District Magistrate, Delhi, Thomas Dana v. State of Punjab, and Mohammed Dastagir v. State of Madras.

predicates.company_affairs_fact_finding_inquiry: The inspector conducted an inquiry to find out how a company’s affairs were managed and whether irregularities occurred.
predicates.person_compelled_to_provide_evidence: The inspector required a person to answer questions or produce documents for the inquiry.
predicates.no_formal_offence_accusation_at_relevant: No formal accusation that the person committed an offence had been made when the person was required to provide evidence.

issues.definition: If a person is compelled to provide evidence in a company-affairs fact-finding inquiry before any formal offence accusation has been made against that person, the compulsion does not violate the protection against self-incrimination.

issues.legal_issue: A distinct investigative regime for companies and their managers does not violate equal protection when their control of the financial interests of many people creates a rational basis for special safeguards against abuse.
material_facts: The challenged investigation provisions applied to companies and persons involved in managing their affairs.
Company managers were entrusted with financial interests affecting creditors, contributors, and others interested in the company.
The provisions withheld from those investigated some protections ordinarily available to witnesses, including protections under the Evidence Act and the Criminal Procedure Code.
issues.conclusion: The investigation provisions did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits class legislation but permits reasonable classification when it rests on an intelligible differentia distinguishing the included group from others and that differentia has a rational relation to the legislative objective. Companies and their managers may be treated as a distinct group because managers control financial interests belonging to many people, and safeguards may address the risk that managers abuse that control. The Court applied Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar and considered the protections otherwise afforded by section 132 of the Indian Evidence Act and section 161(1) and (2) of the Criminal Procedure Code in relation to sections 239 and 240 of the Companies Act, 1956.

predicates.company_management_investigation: The proceeding investigated the management of a company’s affairs.
predicates.managers_control_interests_of_many_peopl: The company’s managers were entrusted with financial interests affecting many creditors, contributors, or other interested persons.
predicates.management_control_can_be_abused_for_per: Persons managing the company could use their position for personal gain at the expense of people interested in the company.

issues.definition: A distinct investigative classification satisfies equal protection when a company-management investigation concerns managers who control the interests of many people and that control can be abused for personal gain.
